newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian killer loses "enzyme defence" appeal.
newsitem.headline: Italian killer loses "enzyme defence" appeal.

text.p: A convicted murderer who asked an Italian court to examine evidence of an enzyme imbalance he said proved he had been temporarily deranged lost his appeal on Friday but had his sentence cut by four years.

Angelo Ortolina, a 41-year-old primary school teacher sentenced to 17 years in jail for the premeditated murder of his mistress in 1995, had asked the Milan appeal court to order a study of his condition by a biological pyschiatrist.
The judges rejected the request but reduced Ortolina's jail term to 13 years. Appeal courts in Italy can reduce or increase sentences at the judges' discretion.
Defence lawyers said they would now take their scientific case to the Court of Cassation, Italy's highest court.

In what they claimed as a forensic first in Italy, the lawyers had told the court that new scientific evidence showed that abnormally high levels of the enzyme creatine kinase (CPK) in a person's blood were a pointer to mental illness.
CPK is an enzyme found in some muscular tissue including the heart.

The lawyers had said high CPK levels in Ortolina's blood at the time he shot his former mistress Maria Antonia Magni showed he had been suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and was therefore incapable of knowing right from wrong.
Ortolina's CPK levels were measured during tests he was having just before the shooting but were not cited as evidence at his trial. The levels returned to normal after the killing.
